paragraphs: §The Blinding of Saul

All this time, Saul was hunting down the Master's disciples like a man on a mission — his mission was to wipe them out. He went to the Chief Priest and got arrest warrants for the meeting places in Damascus: if he found anyone there following the Way, man or woman, he would arrest them and haul them back to Jerusalem.
He headed out. Just outside Damascus, a blinding flash of light exploded around him and knocked him to the ground. Then he heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why are you trying to destroy me?"
"Who are you, Master?" Saul asked. "I am Jesus — the One you're hunting down. Get up and go into the city. Once you're there, you'll be told exactly what to do."

His traveling buddies froze in shock — they heard the voice, but they couldn't see a single person. And Saul, getting up off the ground, discovered he couldn't see a thing. They had to take him by the hand and lead him into Damascus. For three days he stayed blind. He didn't eat. He didn't drink.
Over in Damascus, there was a disciple named Ananias. The Master spoke to him in a vision: "Ananias." "Yes, Master?" he answered.

"Get up and head over to Straight Avenue. At the house of Judas, ask for a guy from Tarsus named Saul. He's there praying. He just had a dream where he saw a man named Ananias walk in, lay hands on him, and give him his sight back."

Ananias pushed back: "Master, you can't be serious. Everyone's talking about this guy and the awful things he's done — the reign of terror he's run against your people in Jerusalem! And now he's here with official papers from the Chief Priest giving him the green light to do the same to us."

But the Master said, "Don't argue with me. Go! I chose him personally to represent me to non-Jews and kings and Jews alike. And I'm about to show him what he's signed up for — the hard suffering that comes with this job."

So Ananias went, found the house, and placed his hands on blind Saul. "Brother Saul," he said, "the Master sent me — the same Jesus you met on the road here. He sent me so you could see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit." Before he even finished talking, something like scales fell off Saul's eyes — and he could see! He jumped to his feet, got baptized, and then sat down with everyone for a huge meal.
§Plots Against Saul

Saul spent a few days hanging out with the Damascus disciples, but he didn't waste any time getting to work. He went straight to the meeting places and started preaching that this Jesus is the Son of God. People were totally thrown — they weren't sure they could trust him. They kept saying, "Hold on, isn't this the guy who tore through Jerusalem hunting believers? Didn't he come here to arrest us and drag us back to Jerusalem for sentencing by the high priests?"

But their doubts didn't slow Saul down one bit. He was on a roll now, and he went right at the opposition — debating the Damascus Jews into a corner and laying out the case that this Jesus is the Messiah.

After this went on for a good long while, some Jews started plotting to kill him — but Saul caught wind of it. They posted guards at the city gates around the clock, waiting to finish him off. So one night, the disciples pulled off a rescue mission and lowered him over the city wall in a basket.

Back in Jerusalem, Saul tried to join the disciples — but they were all terrified of him. Nobody trusted him at all. Then Barnabas stepped in and took him under his wing. He introduced Saul to the apostles and vouched for him, telling them how Saul had seen and talked with the Master on the Damascus road, and how in Damascus he'd risked his life boldly preaching in Jesus' name.

After that, he was in — one of them. He came and went freely in Jerusalem, preaching in the Master's name without holding anything back. But then he crossed paths with a group called the Hellenists. He'd been locked in a running argument with them, and they decided to have him killed. When his friends found out about the plot, they got him out of town fast — took him to Caesarea, then put him on a ship to Tarsus.

With that, things finally calmed down, and the church enjoyed smooth sailing for a while. All across the country — Judea, Samaria, Galilee — the church grew. The believers were filled with a deep reverence for God. The Holy Spirit was right there with them, making them strong. They thrived.
§Tabitha

Peter set out on a road trip to visit all the churches. Along the way he came to Lydda and met with the believers there. He ran into a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed in bed for eight years. Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!" And he did — he jumped right out of bed. Everyone in Lydda and Sharon saw him up and walking around, and it hit them: God is alive and at work among us.

Down the road in Joppa lived a disciple named Tabitha — which means "Gazelle" in our language. She was famous for doing good and helping people out. While Peter was in the area, she got sick and died. Her friends prepared her body for burial and laid it in a cool room.

Some of the disciples heard Peter was nearby in Lydda, so they sent two men to ask if he'd please come right over. Peter got up and went with them immediately. They led him to the room where Tabitha's body lay. Her old friends — mostly widows — were there mourning, showing Peter the clothes and pieces of clothing the Gazelle had made for them while she was alive. Peter asked all the widows to leave the room. Then he knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, "Tabitha, get up."
She opened her eyes, and the moment she saw Peter, she sat up. He took her by the hand and lifted her to her feet. Then he called the believers and the widows back in and showed them she was alive.
Word spread all over Joppa, and many people put their trust in the Master. Peter stayed in Joppa for a long time, staying as a guest at the home of Simon the Tanner.
